extracted.intended_audience: employers filing H-1B cap-subject registrations/petitions, immigration attorneys, and regulatory analysts (including small business stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and analytic criteria for submitting H-1B registrations and cap‑subject petitions, DHS selection/weighting methodology, program‑integrity safeguards, and the regulatory economic / RFA analyses assessing impacts on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valid registration must represent a bona fide job offer
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is revising 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(ii) to clarify that a valid registration must represent a bona fide job offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule requires an H-1B petition filed after registration selection to contain and be supported by the same identifying information and position information, including SOC code, provided in the selected registration and indicated on the LCA used to support the petition (see new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)). Such petition must also include a proffered wage that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage for the corresponding OEWS wage level in the registration for the SOC code in the area(s) of intended employment (see 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(4)(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of registration and petition identifying/position information
rubrics_metrics.description: An H-1B petition filed after registration selection must contain and be supported by the same identifying information and position information provided in the selected registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements include SOC code and the LCA used to support the petition; DHS will enforce that the petition mirrors the selected registration to preserve process integrity (new 8 CFR citations referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proffered wage must equal or exceed prevailing wage indicated in registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must include a proffered wage that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage for the corresponding OEWS wage level indicated in the registration for the SOC code and area(s) of intended employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proffered wage is reduced to an amount equivalent to a lower wage level than indicated on the original registration, USCIS may view that as an attempt to unfairly increase selection odds and may deny subsequent petitions (see new 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS may deny petitions intended to unfairly increase selection odds
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS may deny a subsequent new or amended petition filed by the petitioner, or a related entity, on behalf of the same beneficiary if the filing was part of the petitioner's attempt to unfairly increase the odds of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reducing the proffered wage to an amount equivalent to a lower wage level than indicated on the original registration or petition. Attempting to 'unfairly increase the odds of selection' generally refers to deriving benefit from a higher wage level selection without a bona fide job offer at that wage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of veracity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: As currently required, the entity submitting a registration or petition must certify the veracity of the contents of such submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes this requirement and estimates the final rule could increase denials or revocations; certifying veracity remains a key program‑integrity control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process integrity objective (prevent gaming and ensure bona fide offers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the rule are intended to improve process integrity by aligning registration and petition data and deterring attempts to game selection through inconsistent wages or representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS expects improved program integrity and notes potential increases in denials/revocations though it cannot quantify this impact. Process integrity measures include data alignment, wage-level checks, and certification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted selection objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule implements a weighted selection process to better ensure initial H-1B visas and status grants are more likely to go to the highest skilled or highest paid beneficiaries while not effectively precluding those at lower wage levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS evaluated alternatives but finalized the weighted selection proposed in the NPRM to balance favoring higher-paid/skilled beneficiaries without eliminating opportunities for lower wage levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of alternative weighting schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS considered but declined alternatives such as ranking solely by highest prevailing wage level (2021 rule), partial weighting, geographic/occupation-adjusted weighting, and other commenter-suggested weighted factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for rejection include excessively excluding lower wage levels (2021 approach), limited improvement (partial weighting), unnecessary complexity and susceptibility to gaming (geographic/occupation carveouts), and administrative impracticability or undermining the rule's objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The RFA requires Federal agencies to consider potential impacts of regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and small organizations, and to perform a regulatory flexibility analysis when a rule directly regulates small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis must include a statement of need and objectives, a statement of significant issues raised by public comments and responses, a description and estimate of the number of small entities affected, alternatives considered to minimize impacts, and reporting/recordkeeping/compliance requirements for small entities. The courts interpret 'subject to' as imposing responsibilities directly on the entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification method for 'small entity'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'small entities' comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations independently owned and operated and not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations under 50,000; individuals are not small entities for RFA purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS used NAICS codes and the SBA table of size standards to classify entities by revenue or employee thresholds. For unmatched employers (~20% in DHS data), DHS considered them small if number of employees was less than 500.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate of number of small entities affected
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS must describe and estimate the number of small entities to which the final rule will apply or explain why no estimate is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using FY2024 internal filing data merged with SBA size standards and LCA data, DHS identified 22,453 classified entities of which 76% (17,069) were small entities and estimated 17,069 small entities impacted by the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of small entity economic impact (loss of output method)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS quantifies loss of output to employers who registered at wage level I but were not selected due to the new selection process as a transfer equal to the lost wages of level I workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS used the level I average annual salary ($85,006) to estimate lost output per affected case; internal data show 9,428 unique small entities filed petitions at wage level I in FY2024. DHS divides $85,006 by each entity's revenue to compute percent impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance threshold for small entity impact
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS considers an impact greater than 1 percent of a small entity's revenue as significant for purposes of the RFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying this threshold, DHS estimates 5,193 small entities will experience a cost increase greater than 1% of revenue and 2,665 will experience a cost increase greater than 5% of revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting, recordkeeping, and compliance requirements (scope and skill levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires employers to report additional information (beneficiary's appropriate wage level, SOC code, area of intended employment) in the registration system, on Form I-129, and on the H-1B Data Collection Supplement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS estimates increased burden: submitting an H-1B registration +20 minutes; filing Form I-129 +15 minutes. DHS believes these tasks will be completed by an HR specialist, in-house lawyer, or outsourced lawyer (and provides cost estimates for each).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity cost estimation approach for time burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates time burdens (e.g., 0.25 hours per registration/petition) and multiplies by compensation rates to estimate opportunity costs for in-house and outsourced lawyers and HR specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 17 and Table 18 illustrate population counts (e.g., 336,023 filings with Form G-28), time burden (0.25 hours), hourly compensation rates (example values shown in tables, e.g., $123.02 and $212.10 for lawyers; $53.03 for HR specialists), and resulting total opportunity cost estimates (e.g., $10,334,387; $17,817,620; average $14,076,004; HR specialists $1,149,903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic analysis metrics and methods (costs, benefits, transfers, discounting)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS presents total annual costs, benefits, and transfers annualized over a 10-year period and provides undiscounted and discounted (3% and 7%) estimates of net benefits and transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 10-year undiscounted total net benefits ($19,779,598,238), total estimated benefits ($20,083,219,438), total estimated transfers ($34,338,811,909), and annualized discounted net benefits and transfers (tables provide annual and per‑year breakdowns). Discounting and annualization methods are explicitly applied at 3% and 7% rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee recovery principle under INA sec. 286(m)
rubrics_metrics.description: The INA provides for collection of fees at a level that will ensure recovery of the full costs of providing adjudication and naturalization services by DHS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees are established to recover assigned adjudication costs and unassigned overhead; DHS notes that if the final rule increases costs, fee schedule adjustments will be determined at USCIS's next comprehensive biennial fee review.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRA designation and required delayed effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has determined this final rule is a 'major rule' under the Congressional Review Act (CRA), 5 U.S.C. 804.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a major rule, it requires at least a 60-day delayed effective date; DHS has complied with CRA reporting requirements and sent the final rule to Congress and the Comptroller General.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data matching and classification methodology for regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS's analysis merges internal USCIS filing data with LCA data and SBA size standards to classify petitioning entities and determine wage-level distributions and small-entity impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS used OPQ, CLAIMS3 and ELIS internal data merged with DOL LCA disclosure files and SBA tables; approximately 20% of petitions were unmatched to SBA table and were treated as small if employees <500. The analysis reports counts, wage-level distributions, and top NAICS codes for small entity filers.
